articles.title: Russian bombing kills 26 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
articles.snippet: Local officials say more had been missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit a village in southern Ukraine.
articles.full_text:
Russian bombing kills 26 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
- Published
At least 26 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".
Five people were injured and 27 initially reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.
He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescuer teams searching through the rubble.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Zelensky initially put the death toll at 18, but Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS later said 24 people, including two rescuers and four police officers, were confirmed to have been killed.
In his video address late on Monday, Zelensky said 26 people were now known to have died.
He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday.
"This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."
He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".
"With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.
Meanwhile, Semikin described the Russian attack as a "terrible tragedy" for the village, confirming that "people are still under the rubble".
He said rescue teams were working at the scene, but they had been forced to halt their operation a number of times because of Russian drone attacks in the area.
A day of mourning has been declared for Tuesday across the entire Zaporizhzhia region.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title: Copilot in deadly Florida jet crash identified in reports as 20-year-old
articles.snippet: In air traffic audio, a crew member can be heard shouting: "We are going to crash into the ground!"
articles.full_text:
Copilot in deadly Florida jet crash identified in reports as 20-year-old
- Published
A 20-year-old copilot was among nine people killed when a small jet crashed and exploded in Florida on Sunday, according to US media.
Nathalia Filgueiras, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, is reported to have been one of two crew members aboard the Learjet 60 from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when it crashed near West Palm Beach.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said it would investigate to what extent ice and turbulence may have contributed to the crash, and whether human error played a role.
One man on the ground sustained a leg injury when the aircraft nosedived on to a street near Cresthaven, nine miles (14 km) from President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.
Images from the scene show a large fiery crater in the middle of a residential suburban street.
The debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area, officials told a news conference on Monday, possible evidence that the plane broke up before it hit the ground.
The NTSB confirmed that after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbulence.
"We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000 feet if able," the crew said.
NTSB member Tom Chapman said that less than 30 seconds later, the plane began to descend and the crew issued a mayday call.
The transmission then became "unintelligible", he said, adding that: "Sadly, all aboard were lost."
Flight analysis indicates the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.
In air traffic control audio, a crew member can be heard declaring an emergency, shouting "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".
About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last remark from the cockpit was "we're out of time".
Filgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the fireball.
Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."
In a 2023 interview with a local news affiliate of CBS News, Filgueiras spoke proudly of receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school.
"I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes, but I can't drive a car, I mean I can but, a lot of people think it's funny."
None of the other eight people on board has been identified.
The NTSB said that ice and turbulence were factors in the crash.
Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.
The NTSB said determining the probable cause of the crash will be a "lengthy investigatory process".
As part of the investigation, the NTSB is working with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), representatives from Learjet as well as meteorologists and air traffic control experts.
Recovering the wreckage from the crater on the roadway will be a "daunting challenge", said Timothy Monville, an air safety investigator with the NTSB.
He added that an individual who was in a vehicle near the crash site sustained a leg injury.
Unverified footage posted on social media shows what appears to be a dash-camera recording of the moment of the crash.
"When you see that video, it's a jarring thing," Florida Governor Ron DeSantis told reporters at a news conference on Sunday. "It's like a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere."
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described the crash as a "horrific tragedy".
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the crash happened on Military Trail, a six-lane road lined with businesses and restaurants.
Thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.
Trump was at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday morning, and departed from an airport nearby on Air Force One about an hour before the crash.

articles.title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
articles.snippet: The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C.
articles.full_text:
Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
- Published
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.
In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost â¬100,000 (Â£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".
In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in SjÃ¶bo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.
Additional reporting by Shiona McCallum

articles.title: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
articles.snippet: Though unprecedented, the six-day truce has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that continues to grinds on.
articles.full_text:
Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
- Published
Fighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.
The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.
On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.
Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition.
"The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.
The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping".
"It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.
The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.
An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.
Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.
But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.
In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" â a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday.
And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.
The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.
The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.
Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
"I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV.
"I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."
Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.
But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.
There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residents arrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.
The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.
Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.
As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month.
If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

articles.title: Man guilty of stealing cash from farm owned by South African president
articles.snippet: The case, part of the "Farmgate" scandal, has left President Cyril Ramaphosa mired in an impeachment saga.
articles.full_text:
Man guilty of stealing cash from farm owned by South African president
- Published
A court in South Africa has found a man guilty of stealing more than $500,000 (Â£372,822) in cash from a farm owned by South African president Cyril Ramaphosa, in a case that mired the head of state in an impeachment saga.
Imanuwela David was found guilty of theft on Monday, as well as conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal at Phala Phala farm in the Limpopo province in 2020.
Froliana Joseph, a cleaner at the property, was also found guilty of conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal.
Her brother, Ndilinasho Joseph, was acquitted on all charges.
David was accused of breaking into the cattle farm in February 2020 and taking $580,000 (Â£432,000) in cash from a sofa on the property. David then went on a spending spree, buying a range of cars including three Mercedes - among them one for his girlfriend - a Porsche, two Volkswagens as well as diamond-encrusted Rolex watches and a house.
David told the court he had made the money through businesses including diamonds and Bitcoin, claims the court rejected. The court also found that David was the only one of the two convicted who had any of the stolen cash in his bank account.
Pre-sentencing will take place on 13 November.
There have been many twists and turns in what is known as the Farmgate scandal.
The theft was largely unknown until 2022 when it was brought to light by Arthur Fraser, South Africa's former intelligence chief and an ally for the former president Jacob Zuma, when he claimed that Ramaphosa hid the theft from the police and tax authorities.
Ramaphosa admitted the theft took place but denied any wrongdoing.
An independent panel that same year found Ramaphosa could have questions to answer over the burglary. MPs voted against establishing an impeachment inquiry.
In May this year, the constitutional court ruled that parliament had acted unlawfully by shelving the panel's report, and in July Ramaphosa blocked the parliamentary inquiry through a provincial court.

articles.title: Dutch police offer record €2m reward in hunt for drug lord
articles.snippet: Jos Leijdekkers has been found guilty in absentia of cocaine smuggling and is believed to be in Sierra Leone.
articles.full_text:
Dutch police offer record â¬2m reward in hunt for drug lord
- Published
Dutch authorities have offered a record award of â¬2m (Â£1.7m/$2.24m) for information leading to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers, one of Europe's most-wanted men.
The 35-year-old, who is also known as Bolle Jos (Chubby Jos), was previously accused of being "one of the key players in international cocaine trafficking" by Dutch police.
Commenting on the decision to increase the reward ten-fold, Dutch justice minister David van Weel said it was "necessary given the threat that Leijdekkers poses to national security, our democratic rule of law, and the international legal order".
Dutch prosecutors said capturing Leijdekkers was their "highest priority" and any information shared would be kept secret.
He is listed by Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, as among their most-wanted fugitives.
In January 2025, Dutch police said he was believed to be living in Sierra Leone and going by the name Omar Sherrif.
Images apparently showing Leijdekkers in the company of President Julius Maada Bio and other officials have previously emerged.
Dutch prosecutors have demanded his extradition but Sierra Leone has refused to cooperate, prompting the EU to cut some aid to the country.
West Africa is a major transit point for cocaine trafficking from Latin America.
In 2024, a court in Rotterdam sentenced Leijdekkers in absentia to 24 years in prison after finding him guilty of smuggling â more than seven metric tons of cocaine.
Several other police investigations in the Netherlands are ongoing.
Leijdekkers has also been sentenced to 79 years in prison in Belgium.
Dutch authorities estimate he has made tens of millions of euros from â cocaine smuggling, and accuse him of money laundering and involvement in the use of extreme violence.

articles.title: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
articles.snippet: The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by the US Treasury.
articles.full_text:
Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
- Published
US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.
He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.
The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.
In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights.
The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its alleged role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo.
The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.
For South Africa, the US additionally pointed to corruption.
"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.
The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.
"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.

articles.title: Fake nuclear warning from hacked app sparks unease but not panic in Ukraine
articles.snippet: Many Ukrainians, who have faced years of Russian attacks, did not take the messages seriously and doubted their veracity.
articles.full_text:
Fake nuclear warning from hacked app sparks unease but not panic in Ukraine
- Published
Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian drones and missiles.
On Sunday night, the system delivered something to make them sit up and take note â a succession of more extreme threats that quickly escalated to impending nuclear strikes, chemical attacks and combat on the streets.
But many in the country did not take them seriously and doubted the veracity of the messages.
Sofia Kochmar, 34, a mother-of-one living in the western city of Lviv, said she was initially concerned but quickly questioned the authenticity of the alerts.
"The first thing I saw was the word 'nuclear' and that made me pretty nervous and scared. So my first thought was that something nuclear was actually flying toward us."
"But then the notification mentioned 'street fighting in Kyiv', and I thought, wait, no, that's impossible."
The alerts included some messages written in Russian, and one included a link to a Telegram channel apparently owned by a hacker group.
Within 15 minutes, Ukraine's Air Force issued a statement saying the alert app had been compromised and clarifying there was no radiation threat. But it took more than an hour to issue "all clear" messages.
Anastasiia Romanytska, a 29-year-old ballerina living in Kyiv, said she does not have the alert app installed but friends forwarded her the warnings.
"My first reaction was, 'Is this some kind of joke?' But then my body reacted as if I was under stress. My heart started racing, and my stomach tightened up."
"Still, somehow I immediately realised that it wasn't something serious. Or maybe I just really wanted to believe that."
There are a number of apps delivering phone notifications of air raid warnings, with maps showing areas under threat, all using the same data as the official government-backed app.
Yevhen Baliutov, a cybersecurity expert at Kyiv School of Economics, told the BBC it was clear to him the Ukrainian alert system was hacked by Russians, saying many Ukrainians had clicked a link included with the alerts leading to a Russian Telegram channel, potentially exposing them to further disinformation, phishing attempts or data breaches.
"This is a war, so it's no surprise that Russia will try to hack, will try to send us fake news, will try to manipulate, and will use that for their propaganda."
While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.
Baliutov said it was also logical that Ukraine would have responded by launching a cyber-attack on the Russian emergency alert system. Both sides have similar capabilities in cyber warfare, he added.
Kochmar said after the initial concern, Ukrainians quickly turned to joking about the incident.
"All our work group chats immediately blew up. Everyone started messaging each other, discussing what was happening. And what I found fascinating was how quickly we turned the whole thing into a joke."
Although the impact of this incident had been limited, it illustrated the weakness of a crucial system, Baliutov said.
"It's very dangerous for Ukraine and for our people. When developing such applications, we need to consider security from the very beginning, without skipping essential security measures. When millions of people rely on a service, we cannot afford to take shortcuts with security."
The authorities already faced the challenge of maintaining public alertness after four and a half years of war with ceaseless attack warnings sounding sometimes hourly. Now they must reassure people the systems in place to protect them are robust, trustworthy and should be followed.

HRW calls on Zambia to halt post-election crackdown
Opposition figures arrested and disappeared since President Hakainde Hichilema claimed August victory.
Human Rights Watch (HRW) has called on Zambia’s authorities to halt the vicious clampdown on the political opposition that was launched following President Hakainde Hichilema’s victory in disputed elections in August.
The rights group demanded in a report released on Sunday that the authorities put a stop to the intensifying crackdown.

It accused Zambia’s government of silencing government critics, with several members of the opposition, as well as journalists and lawyers, arrested and some having disappeared in recent months.
“The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices,” HRW said.
The group said that Zambian police and military “forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members and supporters as well as lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August 2026”.
“Zambia’s government should break this dangerous cycle of repression,” added Ashwanee Budoo-Scholtz, deputy Africa director at HRW.
“The authorities should immediately halt the ongoing post-election crackdown, allow access to lawyers and provide medical care for those in detention, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses by security forces.”
Hichilema was sworn in for a second term as Zambia’s president following his victory in August. Critics have insisted that the election was marred by vote rigging.
As he was inaugurated at the National Heroes Stadium in the Zambian capital, Lusaka, his main rival Brian Mundubile was in detention, accused of treason after claiming the opposition had won the election.
Police raided Mundubile’s home the day after the August 13 elections. A former cabinet member, Mutotwe Kafwaya, was shot and killed during the operation.
HRW called on the Zambian authorities to institute an independent, impartial and thorough investigation into the matter.
About a dozen other opposition figures who have questioned the election results have been arrested.
Meanwhile, authorities suddenly closed the country’s courts two weeks after the election, a move that Zambian police stated was an “intelligence-led and preventive measure”, without providing details.
HRW noted that the closure prevents the opposition from filing legal challenges against the vote.

Lindsay Clancy back in court seeking to have murder charges dismissed
Defence argues juror misconduct and judge’s questioning impacted Clancy’s trial for strangling of her three children.
Lindsay Clancy, the American mother facing murder charges for killing her three young children, has returned to court in a bid to get the charges dropped.
Clancy’s lawyers urged Judge William Sullivan on Monday to dismiss the first-degree murder charges against her in the state of Massachusetts in the United States, saying retrying her for killing her three young children would violate her constitutional rights.

Prosecutors said they intend to retry Clancy if the case moves forward but have not decided if she would face the same first-degree murder charges.
Monday’s hearing was her second time in court since September, when jurors were unable to reach a verdict at her trial.
Clancy strangled her three children with exercise bands in 2023 at her home in Duxbury, a suburb of Boston in Massachusetts. Clancy then attempted to take her own life by cutting herself with a knife and was paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window.
At Monday’s hearing, defence lawyer Martin G Weinberg argued that the judge should have investigated further after the jury foreperson sent two notes indicating that a juror was not following the rules. Further questioning could have revealed grounds to remove the juror, identified as Michael Desronvil, and continue deliberations, he said.
After receiving the notes, Sullivan spoke with each juror, reminding them of their duties and explaining what constitutes reasonable doubt in a court case. He asked whether they could apply the law to the case, and all said yes.
But Weinberg argued that Sullivan had not gone far enough. A juror who said he could follow the law could have been lying, Weinberg said, and the situation warranted questioning the foreperson separately to learn more about what was happening during deliberations.
Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague argued there was no indication the holdout juror’s disagreement stemmed from personal bias or an inability to deliberate, rather than a different assessment of the evidence.
Sprague said the judge handled the jury impasse appropriately, saying the fact that one juror dug in his heels did not mean Sullivan should risk interfering with the deliberations by questioning him.
“It is clear from the record this juror did not refuse to deliberate,” Sprague said. “He refused to agree.”
Defence lawyer Kevin Reddington accused the lone holdout juror of using a mobile phone to research terms related to the case and questioned whether he had been truthful during jury selection.
Clancy has never disputed killing her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behaviour. Prosecutors have acknowledged that Clancy, now 36, had mental health problems but said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong.
Sullivan did not immediately rule on the motion to dismiss. He scheduled another hearing for November 16 and suggested a retrial could begin in March.
Another motion expected to be discussed is the state of Massachusetts’s request for a gag order barring lawyers and their supporters “from making extrajudicial statements to the media that would have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceeding”.

Trump asks Supreme Court to block 20,000 California ballots before midterms
California says the move to block ballots from suspected noncitizens could disenfranchise eligible voters.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has asked the Supreme Court to stop California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are not US citizens.
The emergency request, filed on Monday, just one day before the midterm elections, is the latest development in a legal battle between the administration and California, a Democratic stronghold and the most populous US state.
California says the move could disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.
The Department of Justice wants California to set aside ballots from voters on a list compiled by the Department of Homeland Security until after their citizenship status is confirmed.
But California says the list is unreliable and could include thousands of US citizens.
Voting has been under way since early October, and state officials say it would be nearly impossible to separate the ballots in question.
Last week, a federal judge rejected the administration’s request, raising concerns about the reliability of the data on the list.
“If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” Judge David Carter wrote.
The administration has turned to the Supreme Court after a federal appeals court also rejected the request on Friday.
The dispute comes as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress in Tuesday’s elections.
Trump has repeatedly made false claims about widespread voter fraud, but studies and state audits have shown that ineligible voting, including by noncitizens, is rare.

Tehran says plan has been condensed and can be implemented within two days as it continues talks with mediators.
Iran has said it is trying to accelerate the ceasefire plan it has proposed to the United States, as the region braces for possible renewed fighting in the US-Israel war against the country.
Officials in Tehran said on Monday that the seven-step plan they put on the table last month remains the same, but could now be implemented more quickly. The proposal includes a swift reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and return to talks over Iran’s nuclear programme.

The statement comes as Iranian officials continue negotiations with Qatari mediators in the latest effort to find a diplomatic path out of the eight-month conflict.
US President Donald Trump has said the latest negotiations were “going fine” but has suggested several times that the United States could strike Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections.
The offer from Iran remains on the table but has now been “condensed and can be implemented within two days” instead of seven, Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.
“If Iran’s demands are met, it is possible that both security will be restored to the Strait of Hormuz and the negotiation process will begin within a short period of time,” Baghaei said. “All of this depends on how the American side wants to proceed regarding the future of this process.”
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has reportedly granted “powers” to the government to accelerate talks with the US to end the regional war, the state IRNA news agency said.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reiterated that Tehran is prepared for both diplomacy and military confrontation, as mediators Qatar and Pakistan continue to facilitate indirect talks.
“By accepting these conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will be opened and negotiations will resume,” Araghchi told IRNA in Ashgabat, Turkmenistan. “Otherwise, the current situation will continue and Iran will not bow down.”
Iran previously said the plan could be implemented within a week if the US met its conditions, which include lifting the naval blockade of its ports, the repeal of sanctions, and a guarantee of an end to strikes, and a complete regional ceasefire, especially in Lebanon.

German unions launch wave of strikes over cost-of-living pressures
The expanded industrial action comes amid a wave of strikes and protests that have sparked unrest across Europe.
Germany’s largest union has launched a wave of strikes as it pushes for higher wages and increased job security.
The walkouts on Monday escalated a wage dispute affecting about 3.7 million employees in Germany’s metal and electrical engineering industries. The expanded industrial action comes amid myriad strikes and protests across Europe over the cost of living and conditions in workplaces and educational facilities, several of which have seen severe unrest.
Major manufacturers including Audi, Mercedes-Benz and Tata Steel were affected by the strikes launched by the IG Metall union. The union is calling for a 5 percent pay rise amid cost-of-living pressures, as well as measures to protect jobs and production sites, and profit-sharing arrangements in sectors performing strongly.
Employers have proposed a one-off payment equivalent to 1 percent of pay in July 2027, followed by a 1.3 percent wage increase from July 2028. The proposal would allow companies facing financial difficulties to withhold the one-off payment.
IG Metall rejected the offer, saying it would amount to a pay cut in real terms, and called for the expansion of the industrial action.
Strikes are expected to continue throughout the week. The union plans to release participation figures on Friday. During the previous bargaining round in 2024, more than 100,000 workers took part on peak days.
The cost of living, housing costs, and education policy have provoked demonstrations across Europe in recent weeks. Students and unions have led mass rallies, and unrest has rocked Belgium, France and Spain among other countries.
The wave of protest reached Germany over the weekend, with thousands of people rallying in Berlin and more than 30 other German cities on Saturday.

articles.title: Russia is giving its drones bigger antennas to beat Ukrainian jamming
articles.snippet: Kyiv now needs roughly twice as many jammers to stop each upgraded Shahed, intel officials and experts said.
articles.full_text:
KYIV, Ukraine — Russia is fitting drones with larger jam-resistant antennas, making it harder for Ukrainian forces to use electronic countermeasures to scramble their navigation signals, Ukrainian officials said.
Russia’s Kometa navigation modules, produced by the company VNIIR-Progress, use arrays of small receiving elements called patch antennas to keep satellite navigation working through jamming. They have been found on Geran drones, glide-bomb kits, Iskander-M and Kinzhal missiles and the new Filin cruise missile, according to a database of Russian weapons run by Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR.
The Kremlin is already using Kometa modules with 16-element antenna arrays at scale and is setting up serial production of 20-element arrays, increasing its capability to work out which direction jamming comes from and compensate for it, HUR said Oct. 19.
Shaheds carrying antennas with 32 elements have already been found attacking Kyiv, said Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, an electronic-warfare specialist and adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology.
“The more elements, the more electronic-warfare signal sources the antenna can suppress,” he said in an October post on Telegram.
The larger antennas give Russia an asymmetric advantage by being easier to counter than to install, Beskrestnov said.
“This race is difficult for us because it is easier for the enemy to increase the number of elements on an antenna than it is for us to add electronic warfare sites,” Beskrestnov said.
Russia’s better-protected drones can fly through Ukraine’s EW shield — one of its most affordable and widespread layers of air defense — leaving more of them to be shot down by costlier options, like interceptor drones, jets and missiles.
A Kometa module’s resistance to jamming depends on the number and arrangement of its patch antennas, the receiving elements on the array, and on the algorithm its processing chip uses to separate the satellite signal from interference, HUR said.
Drones carrying the upgraded antennas can still be taken out by jamming more satellite bands at once or by networking devices to feed drones false coordinates, defense leaders say.
The commander of Ukraine’s Night Watch unit, who goes by the call sign Alkhimik, bought a 32-element antenna taken from a Shahed, “that had crashed and was being sold on the secondary market,” he told Militarnyi in July.
He discovered that the device was simply two 16-element arrays covering different satellite-navigation bands put together, he said, giving him inspiration on how to counter it.
“By creating two systems — one operating in the L1 band and the other covering L2/L5 — we’ll be able to jam this antenna without any problems,” Alkhimik said.
Spoofing works, too, according to Fly Group Ukraine. It links multiple devices into a network to feed a drone false coordinates, Anatoliy Khrapchynskyi, the defense company’s director of development, told Reuters in September.
“The drone continues to think it is flying toward its target, but its own autopilot, relying on the false coordinates, gradually changes course on its own and steers the craft away from cities into safe areas,” he said.
Russian defense firms have ordered more than 100,000 Kometa modules in various configurations this year to guide cruise and ballistic missiles, strike drones and guided bombs, HUR said, a measure of demand for the technology.

articles.title: US approves $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
articles.snippet: The missiles — which are yet to be manufactured — are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. State Department said on Friday it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, in what would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second Trump administration.
Delayed missile deliveries have added to Ukraine’s tensions with the U.S. after President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
On Thursday, a Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed one person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.
Zelenskiy said on Monday that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for the U.S. to sign off on critical missile supplies, as Russia stepped up attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure.
But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will likely not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfill, and two people briefed on the U.S. decision said the missiles — which are yet to be manufactured — are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense is encouraging the Pentagon to bring forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the U.S. arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US JUMPSTART, along with national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in a statement.
The program uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defense following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
The JUMPSTART program was used in August to buy 3,350 air-launched cruise missiles worth $825 million made by Zone 5 Technologies and CoAspire.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The U.S. has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defense and precision-guided weapons.
In July, the U.S. Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $58.6 billion to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.
Lockheed has said that deal would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 MSE production capacity by the end of 2030 and increase jobs at its Camden, Arkansas, plant by 50%, to about 1,850 from 1,200. Lockheed previously announced Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would go to 2,000 units annually.
Pentagon negotiators are pressing contractors to move much faster, with tentative production agreements struck earlier this year at the center of efforts to increase missile output.

articles.title: US greenlights 500 Patriot missiles for Ukraine, with $2.1 billion to be paid by allies
articles.snippet: The announcement comes amid heightened tensions between Kyiv and Washington, including purported delays in the transfer of interceptors.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The State Department announced today that it has approved the potential sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, with an estimated price tag of $2.1 billion to be paid “entirely by partners and allies.”
“The Government of Ukraine has requested to buy five hundred (500) PATRIOT Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) missiles” along with classified and unclassified parts, according to a State Department congressional notification posted online.
The notification said that Kyiv could buy the high-tech missiles “with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan. No U.S. funds are involved in this sale.” JUMPSTART refers to the Joint Ukrainian Multinational Program–Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline program, established in 2022 as a mechanism for third-party countries to contribute funds to allow Ukraine to buy American equipment.
The potential sale “will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe,” the notice says.
However, the diplomatic language belies lingering tensions between Kyiv and Washington, especially when it comes to Patriot missiles. On Oct. 19, The Washington Post reported that the US appeared to have delayed the transfer of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine amid a falling out between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. A few days earlier, CNN reported that Kyiv had run out of interceptors, leaving the country more vulnerable to deadly Russian missile and drone attacks.
On Oct. 25, Zelenskyy said Ukraine and the US had resolved two other recent sticking points — the surprise disruptions in Starlink/Starshield connectivity and in US-provided missile warning information — but he appeared to call out the US for dragging its feet on Patriot deliveries.
“The issue of air defense remains. There is progress on missiles for Patriot systems, but things are moving very slowly. More slowly than Russian missiles fly,” he said. “You cannot say, ‘Yes, we will give the missiles to you,’ and then not deliver them for a month or two. It simply does not work that way.”
The embattled leader previously told ABC News that Ukraine would need 350 interceptors per month to properly defend its territory.
Foreign Military Sales notifications are generally early steps in what can be years-long processes, and today’s announcement is unlikely to solve Kyiv’s short-term air defense issues. After publication of this report, a State Department spokesperson noted that the announcement is a “new proposed sale that is unrelated to prior sales of air defense munitions already in progress.”
FMS deals are also typically not final when they’re announced, as quantities and prices can change as contract negotiations continue. Additionally lawmakers could step in and delay or block the deal as well, though that is less likely in this case considering the remaining bipartisan support for Ukraine.
UPDATED 11/2/2026 at 7:57am ET to include a comment from a State Department spokesperson.

articles.title: Tiny Ukrainian receiver intercepts Russian drone feeds in real time
articles.snippet: A small new receiver can co-opt video from Russian unmanned systems, allowing Ukrainian drone operators to intercept enemy live feeds in real time, the device's makers said this month.
articles.full_text:
KYIV, Ukraine — A new pocket-sized receiver can co-opt video from Russian unmanned systems, allowing Ukrainian drone operators to intercept enemy live feeds in real time, the device’s makers said this month, while adding only a little extra weight to operators’ kits.
Kyiv communications-equipment maker CODE380 developed the D·Vision SDR, which uses a software-defined radio (SDR) to sweep frequencies from 500 megahertz to 8.7 gigahertz for drone signals and convert them into video, reducing common visibility problems and allowing easy software updates for new drone specs.
The D-Vision SDR scans its frequency range without “blind spots” and offers greater sensitivity than competing detectors, the developers told the Ukrainian tech outlet DOU on Oct. 17.
The receiver joins a growing set of cheap, passive Ukrainian drone sensors that listen for threats without emitting a signal that could give away a unit’s position, working alongside radar, acoustic sensors and interceptors rather than replacing them.
CODE380’s device can display analog video from drones up to 6 miles (10 kilometers) away on frequencies between 540 megahertz and 6 gigahertz, and from 2 to 3 miles (3.5 to 5 kilometers) away on higher frequencies, according to manufacturer figures reported by Militarnyi.
Analog drones broadcast their camera feed unencrypted, so a receiver tuned to the right frequency can show a unit where an attack is heading and what the pilot is aiming at before impact.
The receiver’s sweep covers the 4.1 to 4.5 gigahertz band where Russia’s Molniya strike drones began sending video in June, according to Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, presidential adviser and radio specialist.
“Most detectors don’t see these frequencies, or see them poorly,” he wrote in June. “I’m warning you so that trust in a detector doesn’t cost you your life.”
The D-Vision SDR is not the first Ukrainian receiver to tap drone video, but its receiver weighs less than half as much as its main domestic rivals at roughly 10 ounces (290 grams).
Babai’s roughly 2-pound (0.9-kilogram) Vydun 7.5 intercepts analog video up to 7.5 gigahertz, while Contra-drone’s 21-ounce (600-gram) SENSE-4 reaches 8.2 gigahertz and BlueBird Tech’s Chuyka 3.0, which weighs up to 23 ounces (650 grams), can now be upgraded to 8.8 gigahertz, according to manufacturers.
Many receivers struggle to decode digital video, detect Mavic-compatible signals beyond a few miles, and pick up fiber-optic drones guided by cables.
Drone variants are already being designed with harder-to-hack video feeds, Beskrestnov said, pointing out Russia’s Molniyas as an example.
“We need to be ready for digital video to one day fully replace analog,” he wrote, warning that portable detectors and fixed analog receiving stations would then become ineffective.

articles.title: Oshkosh partners with startup to build military drones
articles.snippet: Oshkosh Defense partnered with Grid Aero to scale production of the Lifter aircraft, marking the defense giant's first foray into aircraft manufacturing.
articles.full_text:
Oshkosh Defense announced Monday a partnership with Silicon Valley startup Grid Aero to manufacture large military drones, which would be the first aircraft produced by the Wisconsin-based company.
“We do things that like gravity and stay on the ground,” said Logan Jones, Oshkosh’s chief growth officer, in an interview with Defense News, describing the company’s typical offerings. But he called the partnership “a very nice fit for us.”
Jones said the partnership grew out of the Defense Department’s Arsenal of Freedom campaign, which aims to expand the domestic industrial base. Grid Aero needed a partner to help scale production, while Oshkosh was looking to manufacture something with long-term potential.
“We looked where both the market was growing, and where the technology class would benefit from scale,” he said, explaining why the company has been exploring unmanned systems. Oshkosh was drawn to Grid Aero in part because its Lifter aircraft uses metal construction rather than composite materials, aligning with Oshkosh’s manufacturing capabilities.
Although Oshkosh would technically be considered a subcontractor, Jones said the companies describe the arrangement as a partnership because Oshkosh is helping Grid Aero reconfigure the Lifter aircraft “to ensure that manufacturability is at the heart of their design and strategy from day one, not an afterthought.”
However, Oshkosh wasn’t the only company making a decision. For Grid Aero, Oshkosh’s extensive experience in defense manufacturing helped solidify the decision to work together, co-founder and CEO Arthur Dubois said.
“They build vehicles by the thousands, and that is the rate we need. Their lines are also built for variety. A single Oshkosh line can build many variants of a vehicle, each set up for a different mission, without slowing down. Lifter works the same way,” Dubois said in an email to Defense News.
Founded in 2024, Grid Aero developed the Lifter, an autonomous aircraft with modular payload capacity that the company describes as a “pickup truck of the skies.” The Lifter falls into the Group 4 or Group 5 category of unmanned aerial systems, classifications that cover aircraft weighing more than 1,320 pounds.
Dubois said Oshkosh’s manufacturing technology is a good fit for the Lifter because it is “simple, rugged, piston-powered, and made from ubiquitous materials.” He added that the Lifter’s design “borrows as much from military trucks as from traditional aircraft.”
The companies plan to build thousands of Lifter aircraft for the Defense Department and commercial customers. Initially, Grid Aero will conduct low-rate production while Oshkosh establishes a pilot production line.
“As customer demand grows, we will move production to Oshkosh in stages and keep pace with what the customer needs,” Jones said. “As [the Defense Department] plans for future conflicts, the ability to field and replace aircraft at scale is one of the most important advantages it can build.”

articles.title: Industry needs more consistent demand signal to scale UGV production: Autonomy consortium exec
articles.snippet: “I think [industry has] the challenge of understanding what the demand signal is, and then again where to put their dollars,” Warren Sponsler, the COO of NAMC, said in an interview.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Army’s goal of scaling unmanned ground vehicles is being sabotaged by the service’s inability to provide clear, coherent demand signal to industry, according to the head of the National Advanced Mobility Consortium (NAMC), a nonprofit organization bridging the Pentagon and industry for ground drone projects.
“I think [industry has] the challenge of understanding what the demand signal is, and then again where to put their dollars. We do talk a lot about these capabilities that the Army has asked for, but they [industry] want to know what’s next,” Warren Sponsler, NAMC’s CEO, said in a recent interview.
“[Industry is] trying to align themselves to what’s next. I think that’s probably one of the biggest challenges — just being able to produce at scale.”
Oftentimes companies order parts and put stress on their supply chains before the Army has settled on a contract mechanism or specific capability, Sponsler said. The commitment from industry is there, but the commitment from the Army, or any service for that matter, is not distinct, Sponsler said, which can be rather discouraging for companies.
READ MORE: Is the Pentagon’s demand signal for drones working? It depends on who you ask.
“Following through on those programs, I think it is critical to maintain that relationship between government and industry,” Sponsler said.
Exercises also sometimes send a murky demand signal, Sponsler said. While the Army has invited industry to demonstrate ground autonomy platforms at several events, the sheer amount of opportunities and unclear mission objectives leave companies unsure where to invest their time and money.
“I think it’s kind of the opposite challenge in many cases,” Sponsler said when asked if he thinks there are enough Army exercises for industry to demo their platforms. “There are so many opportunities right now, and then companies, especially those small companies, are having to make often hard decisions as to which experiments they participate in, and which ones they choose not to.”
He added that “focusing some of the demonstration experimentation activities would be a help” to provide a clear demand signal.
“There’s a lot of opportunities right now that the Army talks about for robotics and autonomy companies to get their stuff out in the field, get user feedback, and I think what [industry] is looking for is, ‘What is that path to scaling? Like, where is that path to revenue?’
“The more that they can describe what capabilities they’re actually looking to field and put together, the better,” he said.
Programs Of Record
Sponsler said the Army’s venture capital acquisition hub, FUZE, has provided a strong example through its xTech competitions for how the service should focus its demonstrations on certain capabilities. For example, xTech has held demonstrations, which are a part of larger competitions that will result in contract awards, for autonomous logistics and sustainment projects and for autonomous breaching. The path to revenue is clear in such cases as companies know they could be the winner of an eventual contract.
Sponsler said he urges companies, especially the nontraditionals, to enter such competitions, but he also urges them pay close attention to the Army’s programs of record for ground autonomy as they are the most indicative of how the Army plans to spend its money. The challenge there: the Army’s programs of record for ground autonomy have also fallen prey to the same lack of clarity as its outreach to industry.
For example, within roughly 18 months, the Army altered its UxS program of record and transformed the former Robotic Combat Vehicle program into the Unmanned Ground Commercial Robotic Vehicle program but then dispersed that program into Project Sustainment and the Engineer Autonomous Breaching Capability program.
The service also relocated its acquisition office for autonomy then stood up a separate Portfolio Acquisition Executive for autonomy and redesignated its Futures and Concepts Command as the new Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command (FASCOM), which will work in coordination with the Pentagon’s newly established Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM).
The good news, Sponsler said, is that he believes the new AUTOWARCOM, which has yet to be formally established since it requires Congressional approval, and FASCOM will allow the Army and the Pentagon’s autonomy efforts to be better streamlined.
He said the new organizations will help in “providing additional focus to robotics and autonomy integration at the formation level, looking beyond a product and more to a capability,” Sponsler said.
“[It] should also help to align resources and leadership to best prioritize based on the services’ needs. As the Army operates in multiple domains — ground, air, sea — having a [DoD]-level organization with a vision across services should help to mitigate duplicative efforts and better align resources,” he added.

articles.title: The fiscal risks of bringing US troops out of Europe
articles.snippet: Reducing America’s military footprint in Europe may seem fiscally prudent, but relocating troops and giving up overseas bases could leave US taxpayers with a much bigger bill.
articles.full_text:
The Pentagon is in the final weeks of a 6-month review of the US military footprint overseas, and is reportedly considering major cuts to American forces based in Europe. Cutting the number of US troops based in Europe could be risky for several reasons — it could undermine the extended US nuclear deterrent, send the wrong signal to Moscow and ultimately weaken the stability and security of a region vital to US prosperity.
But there is also a serious fiscal concern that would come with such realignment. Finding space to house tens of thousands of redeployed US troops and their families somewhere across the 50 states won’t be easy, quick or cheap. Meanwhile, future US power projection would become more expensive as military facilities are vacated and returned to our European allies.
In short, even if one overlooks the strategic risks of backing away from Europe while Russia appears more aggressive than ever, the fiscal costs could be too large to ignore.
The unfolding posture review undertaken by the Department of Defense is expected to wrap up in early November. Reportedly, dramatic cuts to the number of US troops based in and/or rotated to Europe are under consideration. In comparison to the height of the Cold War — when the United States maintained nearly half a million troops in Europe — today there are about 80,000 US troops there. Roughly 65,000 of these are in Europe on typical 3-year assignments with dependents, while about 15,000 are in Europe on shorter heel-to-toe rotational deployments without dependents.
Rotationally-deployed troops are typically sent to Europe for nine months, after which they are replaced by another unit of similar size and capability for the next nine months. These persistent rotational deployments started as a response to Russia’s first invasion of Ukraine in 2014, and have been used primarily to augment the forward-stationed troops in Europe, ensuring a routine American presence across NATO’s eastern allies, which are those most exposed to Russia’s aggression.
The Department of Defense has already trimmed the number of US troops on the ground in Europe, announcing late last year the elimination of a rotationally-deployed infantry brigade (about 4,000 troops) to Romania and southeastern Europe. That deployment was relatively easy to turn off, given the process the Pentagon has used to renew it periodically and the fact that those forces were not accompanied by dependents.
Earlier this year, the Defense Department attempted to cancel another deployment, this one a rotationally-deployed armored brigade typically sent to Poland and northeastern Europe. After Poland’s president weighed in with President Donald Trump, the decision was reversed.
Shortly thereafter, news broke that there were plans inside the department to implement even deeper cuts to US presence in Europe, without conducting any kind of a study or review along the lines of what Congress requires of the administration if it seeks to reduce US troops levels below 76,000. In the wake of the Poland misstep, the more formal process that is now nearing its end was announced, apparently with an eye on fulfilling at least one of the Congressional requirements.
Another is coordination with allies, and in August the administration sent a questionnaire to other members of NATO on their support for US basing and American foreign policy more broadly. When considered alongside the recent call by the Pentagon for state leaders to bid on hosting a new military base – necessary if thousands of US troops and dependents relocate from Europe to America – it seems clear that deep cuts are not merely possible, but rather likely.
Cost Imposition
There are a number of ways that removing forces out of Europe could hit taxpayers in their wallets.
First, there are geopolitical realities. A significant downsizing of US forces in Europe at a time when Russia’s war in Ukraine rages and its hybrid attacks against the West ramp up is likely to only incentivize Moscow in its efforts to undermine security and stability in Europe. If Moscow succeeds, a destabilized, insecure Europe – still America’s most important trade and investment partner – will inevitably impact the livelihoods of average Americans.
However, there are other, more immediate costs to consider. Based on historic data of what the Pentagon paid between 2005 and 2011 to expand Fort Bliss so that it could accommodate an additional 25,000 troops, building additional facilities to host 15-25,000 US troops, plus their dependents, is likely to cost at least $8 billion, in inflation-adjusted terms.
Additionally, if US troops depart Europe, Washington will likely give up the European facilities that hosted them, which means losing access to bases that enable cheaper power projection.
Take for example the attacks on Iran in recent months. Roundtrip bombing missions from the United States to Iran take about 36 hours, while bombing missions from the United Kingdom take as little as 15 hours roundtrip. Given the cost of operating B-1 and B-52 bombers ($97,600/hour and $66,700/hour, respectively), flying from the UK saved the US taxpayer $2.05 million for each B-1 sortie and $1.4 million for each B-52 sortie. By early April, the United States had conducted 62 bombing missions against Iran, only 18 of which had left from North America. If we assume the remainder flew from Europe, which seems likely, the American taxpayer saved about $75 million in just the first five weeks of the war against Iran by having access to bases in Europe.
Reducing US force posture in Europe – for example, to shift some assets to the Pacific – may make sense. But doing so now carries significant strategic risk vis-à-vis Russia and the security of a continent that remains vital to American prosperity. Moreover, it also likely means higher fiscal cost at a time when US debt already seems insurmountable.
John R. Deni is a research professor at the US Army War College, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a nonresident senior fellow at the NATO Defense College. The views expressed are his own.

articles.title: Saab unveils new speed assault boat for Swedish Navy
articles.snippet: “The CB90CX is designed for uncrewed operations from the outset,” Anders Hellman, head of Saab’s business unit in Docksta, told Breaking Defense.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — Swedish defense manufacturer Saab has unveiled the Combat Boat 90 (CB90) CX, a drone boat designed to strike targets beyond the horizon and counter short-range aerial threats, to equip the Swedish Navy.
The company introduced the new speed assault boat Sunday morning before the Euronaval defense show taking place in Paris this week. The CB90CX is designed to operate entirely without a human crew on board, according to Saab, and is promoted as a larger, heavier payload platform than the existing 16.3m-long CB90 Next-Generation (CB90 NG), which is already in service with nine navies globally.
“One of the key distinctions is that the CB90 NG can be upgraded for optionally crewed operations, whereas the CB90CX is designed for uncrewed operations from the outset,” Anders Hellman, head of Saab’s business unit Docksta, told Breaking Defense today.
The CB90CX is 18m long, and according to Hellman, its larger hull increases payload capacity by over 50 percent. He added that it is also integrated with an entirely new vessel infrastructure, which includes an integrated ship automation and monitoring system, fire control system, and steer-by-wire technology.
The new CB90 CX is envisioned to be available in three configurations: an intelligence and surveillance variant relying on Saab’s Giraffe 1X radar; an anti-ship warfare role to enable beyond-line-of-sight strikes against surface vessels; and a short-range air defense variant. The air defense variant will be made possible by equipping the boat with an anti-aircraft automatic cannon that could down uncrewed threats such as drones, according to the manufacturer.
“The capabilities offered through our proposed configurations are well-aligned with the broader operational requirements and future direction outlined in the Swedish Armed Forces Amphibious Battalion 2030 concept,” Hellman said.
The Amphibious Battalion 2030 concept is a modernization program that seeks to shift the Scandinavian country’s traditional coastal defense strategy toward a more mobile, dispersed maritime force. In practice, this means that rather than adopting larger platforms, naval units will use smaller, fast platforms intended to be scattered across the islands and shallow waters of the Baltic Sea and Nordic archipelagos.
The craft is already under production, destined for the Swedish Navy as the launch customer. Hellman could not disclose delivery timelines, only that these will “co-exist” with the service’s existing CB90 NG boats.
In Q2 of 2025, the Swedish Defence Material Administration, or FMV, placed an order for 22 CB90NGs, valued at about 900 million SEK ($92 million). It was intended to replace some of the 16 CB90s the country has provided to the Ukrainian Armed Forces, as part of previous support packages.

articles.title: Greece inks deal for KC-390 fleet
articles.snippet: The purchase, arranged via a government-to-government agreement between Greece and Portugal, covers three KC-390 aircraft with options for up to six manufactured by Brazilian planemaker Embraer.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — Greece has finalized a deal for a new fleet of up to six KC-390 Millennium aircraft, capping an anticipated sale of the airlifter to Athens and setting a first delivery for next year, Greek Defense Minister Nikoloas Dendias and Brazilian manufacturer Embraer revealed today.
The finalized deal, which includes three aircraft with options for three more, was announced by Dendias as part of a visit from his counterpart, Portuguese Minister of National Defense Nuno Melo. The agreement follows the reported approval in June by a Greek parliament committee for the procurement and follow-on support of three Millennium aircraft, with an expected budget of roughly €600 million ($672 million).
The purchase of the Embraer aircraft “marks two firsts” for the Hellenic Air Force, Dendias said, according to a Google translation of his remarks released by the Greek Ministry of National Defense: the acquisition of a “jet transport aircraft,” as well as a refueling tanker. Once fielded by the Hellenic Air Force, the Millennium can refuel Greek fighter jets using a hose-and-drogue system, which Dendias called a “huge advantage.”
Athens plans to acquire the KC-390 via a government-to-government agreement with Portugal, which Dendias confirmed in July. Last year, in addition to upping its own Millennium buy to six aircraft, Lisbon announced options for an additional ten aircraft that could be shared among other NATO members.
“We are honored by Greece’s decision to acquire the KC-390 Millennium. This choice underscores the trust and confidence that leading NATO members place in our aircraft,” Bosco Da Costa Junior, the president and CEO Embraer’s defense unit, said in a company press release.
In his remarks, Dendias noted that Portugal will help Greece effectively wield its forthcoming fleet, including for training and operations. Dendias described the aircraft’s significance in world-historical terms, asserting the Turkish invasion of Cyprus in 1974 — a long-simmering tension between the two NATO countries — “could not have happened” if the Hellenic Air Force possessed a tanker aircraft that capable of refueling its fighter jets.
The sale of the KC-390 marks the seventh European customer for Embraer, which has developed a strong market among NATO nations. Like other international customers, Athens was swayed to replace its aging Lockheed Martin C-130H fleets with the Millennium, which often competes against the newer C-130J. The aircraft can move cargo in addition to refueling among other applications.
The Greek finalized order adds a third customer this year for the Millennium, following deals announced by Colombia and the United Arab Emirates. The Brazilian planemaker eventually hopes to break into the US market with the KC-390 and has offered a dedicated American final assembly line to sweeten the bid.
In the meantime, Embraer plans to ramp production of the C-390 amid higher global demand, aiming for an annual output of 10 aircraft by the end of the decade.

articles.title: Oshkosh steps into large UAS space with new Grid Aero partnership
articles.snippet: The two companies plan to team up on “design for manufacturability, production planning, supply chain optimization, and ultimately building Lifter aircraft at scale.”
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Oshkosh Defense is teaming up with autonomous aircraft firm Grid Aero, in a partnership aimed at scaling up production on the latter’s Lifter drone, the companies announced Monday.
The partnership comes as the Pentagon is pushing for affordable Group 4 and 5 unmanned autonomous systems (UAS) — like Grid Aero’s Lifter, the design of which was unveiled last August — that are produced at scale and that it can purchase in bulk.
“This partnership represents a new model for defense innovation, bringing Silicon Valley’s transformative technology development together with the Midwest’s unmatched manufacturing capability,” Logan Jones, chief growth officer of Oshkosh Defense, said in a statement today. “Grid Aero brings cutting-edge autonomous aircraft innovation, and Oshkosh brings the industrial capability to make it real at scale. Together, we’re addressing critical defense needs with American innovation and American manufacturing.”
Specifically, the two companies plan to team up on “design for manufacturability, production planning, supply chain optimization, and ultimately building Lifter aircraft at scale,” according to an Oshkosh news release.
Arthur Dubois, CEO of Grid Aero, said the Lifter aircraft is designed to haul a “few” thousand pounds, for a “few” thousand miles, and take on a variety of mission sets, ranging from intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), to hauling cargo.
“Our objective is to be as modular as we can with the payload integration systems, whether it’s for cargo, ISR, even other purposes,” Dubois told Breaking Defense. “I’m not going to tell you that we’re designing it for any one specific purpose. We’re designing it to be just like modular pickup truck that you know can have anything mounted on top of it.”
Ultimately, the goal is to produce hundreds, if not thousands, of these aircraft by the early 2030s, according to Dubois.
Dubois estimated there are another six to 12 months of testing for the variety of Lifter prototypes that are being built or are in the works at the moment. In roughly a year, he said he expects that the two companies will launch a pilot line at Oshkosh.
Grid Aero will hash out some design alterations with Oshkosh as they work in tandem to “redesign the platform into its next iteration,” Dubois said. Even so, Dubois said he expects the aircraft to largely maintain its original shape — although there may be some changes related to the parts used to build the aircraft.
“The start of this collaboration is us revisiting the design of the airframe, and working with Oshkosh’s team on supply chain, working on what parts we can actually buy in those volumes, working on what methods actually would work at the the kind of rates we want to build at, working on what Oshkosh’s workforce knows how to do to better integrate that into the design,” Dubois said.
Oshkosh Defense is known for building military vehicles, including Joint Light Tactical Vehicles. Grid Aero emerged from stealth in August 2025, and is based in California.
